blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A planner must pick exactly one of three plans, scored (9, 1), (1, 9) and (4, 4) on two measures to maximize. What is true of (4, 4)?

options.text: It is dominated, since each other plan scores more in total
options.says: Dominance compares measure by measure: (4, 4) has more of the second than (9, 1) and more of the first than (1, 9).

options.text: It is picked at a share of 0.5, since it balances the two measures
options.says: At 0.5 the other two score 5 each and (4, 4) scores 4, as in the three-plan table.

options.text: It is Pareto optimal, and no weighting of the two measures picks it
options.says: Right: nothing dominates it, and the better of the other two always scores at least 5.

options.text: It is picked at some share, since every Pareto-optimal plan is supported
options.says: That holds for linear programs; with a pick-one choice, unsupported Pareto points exist, as here.

origin.section: A Supported Point Is One Some Weighted Sum Returns

questions.stem: On a two-objective front, plans a = (10, 50) and b = (30, 10) are supported, and plan q = (20, 25) is dominated by no plan. Which conclusion is right?

options.text: No share picks q, since q lies below the line from a to b
options.says: Right: the line is at 30 where q has 20 of the first measure, so any share that beats a loses to b.

options.text: A share of 0.5 picks q, since q lies halfway between a and b
options.says: At 0.5, q scores 22.5 while a scores 30; being halfway in one measure is not being on the line.

options.text: Some share picks q, since no plan dominates q
options.says: Being unbeaten makes q Pareto optimal, not supported; the two inequalities in the lesson show no share works.

options.text: A share of 1 picks q, since q has more of the first measure than a
options.says: At a share of 1 only the first measure counts, and b has more of it than q.

origin.section: No Weight Reaches a Point Below the Segment Between Its Supported Neighbours

questions.stem: A two-objective selection model is solved with its binary variables relaxed to the interval [0, 1]. How many of the relaxed model's Pareto points are unsupported?

options.text: More than before, since the relaxed model has more solutions to compare
options.says: More solutions fill the gaps: averages of solutions sit on the segments that left points unsupported.

options.text: As many as before, since the two objectives are the same
options.says: The objectives are the same but the feasible set is not; the integer restriction is what created the gaps.

options.text: Fewer but always some, since a relaxed front still has gaps between plans
options.says: A linear program's reachable values form a convex set, so its front has no gaps (Isermann's theorem).

options.text: None at all, since any average of two relaxed solutions is feasible
options.says: Right: averages are feasible, so no point lies below a segment of two others, and every Pareto point is supported.

origin.section: Integer Variables Create Unsupported Points; an LP Has None
